title: Compare two cases side by side
statement: Teach a relationship by presenting two cases together with an explicit prompt to compare them; two cases met in turn without the prompt work no better than one.
detail: Lesson research on teaching two episodes together found strong evidence that comparing two cases produces relational learning that one case does not. In the core study, children shown one standard took the object match, while those shown two standards together with a prompt to compare them took the relational match; those shown the two in sequence without a prompt preferred object matches, like those shown only one. The research cites a further study in which comparison training beat matched single-item training on learning and far transfer of relational categories, and concludes that a lesson built page by page must put both cases on one page with an explicit instruction to compare.
against: The core study, including its no-prompt condition, used preschoolers (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/research/g4-u1-l3-circe-and-the-lotus-eaters.md`, lines 409-418); the wider claim rests on the comparison-training study the research cites.

evidence.quote: "preschoolers who were shown the two standards sequentially without a prompt to compare them preferred object matches, as did those who viewed only one standard. In contrast, those who saw the exemplars together, with a prompt to compare them, showed the same elevated relational responding" (Christie and Gentner 2010, https://cogdevsoc.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/Christie-Gentner-2010.pdf, journal version https://doi.org/10.1080/15248371003700015).
The condition is the load-bearing part. Two cases read one after another, with no prompt to compare, performed no better than one case.
